analysis.one_liner: Allows Americans to import lower-priced prescription drugs from licensed Canadian pharmacies and wholesalers.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote in the House before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the FDA to write rules within 180 days letting wholesale drug distributors, pharmacies, and individual patients import certain prescription drugs from Canada, and later from other countries with comparable drug-safety systems. It would certify foreign sellers, require valid US prescriptions, allow lab testing of imported drugs, and make it illegal for drug manufacturers to raise prices to Canadian sellers or cut off supply specifically to block imports. It never moved past the House Energy and Commerce Committee's health subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay high prices for prescription drugs, especially people buying insulin, dialysis solution, biologics, and other expensive maintenance medications, since the same drug is often sold for much less in Canada. Wholesale distributors and pharmacies could import lower-cost supplies and pass savings to customers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients paying high US drug prices

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to issue regulations within 180 days permitting importation of qualifying prescription drugs from Canada by wholesalers, pharmacies, and individuals, with expansion to other countries after two years if Canada importation produced savings and safe access.
Lets individuals import up to a 90-day personal supply from a certified foreign pharmacy with a valid US prescription, a channel that does not exist today outside narrow exceptions.

Makes it unlawful for drug manufacturers to charge certified Canadian sellers more than domestic Canadian buyers, restrict or delay their supply, or make the US version of a drug different in order to defeat importation — provisions aimed at the tactics manufacturers have used to neutralize importation.

Adds safety controls: foreign sellers must be licensed, at least five years old, subject to quality-assurance testing and recall cooperation; importers must report prices and transactions to HHS; and the FDA can suspend any seller, importer, or drug over safety problems. It also adds criminal penalties of up to 10 years or $250,000 for websites selling counterfeit or adulterated drugs.
Includes insulin, dialysis solution, biologics, and other high-cost drugs for importers, and explicitly preserves all state and federal legal remedies, so consumers keep their right to sue.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose US prices depend on keeping other countries' lower prices from flowing back into the American market. They would face import competition plus new anti-price-discrimination and anti-supply-restriction rules. The FDA would also bear the cost of certifying foreign sellers, funded by seller fees.

drawbacks.text: Safety critics argue importation opens a channel for counterfeit, substandard, or improperly stored drugs; the bill responds with seller certification, testing, and suspension authority, but no screening regime is airtight and enforcement would fall on an FDA with finite resources.

A 180-day deadline to stand up a full certification and testing program is aggressive, and the bill's ban on manufacturers restricting supply to Canada could strain Canada's own drug supply or simply be difficult to enforce against global manufacturers.

Savings for consumers are not guaranteed: if import volumes stay small, or if manufacturers restructure distribution, most patients would see little price relief while the regulatory system still has to be built and policed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients facing US drug prices that are often far higher than Canadian prices for the same product, the potential benefit is large and direct. The main honest cost is safety risk and administrative burden, which the bill works hard to contain through certification, testing, tracing, and suspension powers. The design is more cautious than a blanket opening of the border, but its effectiveness depends entirely on how aggressively the FDA writes and enforces the rules.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat with no markup, no vote, and no floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Elijah Cummings introduced the bill on January 10, 2019 with 26 original cosponsors, all House Democrats.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction.
On January 25, 2019 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action appears in the record for the remainder of the 116th Congress.
The bill attracted no Republican cosponsors and never received a committee markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who kept the US market closed to Canadian-priced imports for another two years without having to fight the bill on the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 27 named supporters were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Democratic chair of Energy and Commerce allowed no committee action, so the bill died without a partisan floor fight.

industries.note: Importation would bring Canadian-priced versions of their drugs into the US market, and the bill specifically outlaws the price hikes, supply restrictions, and product differences manufacturers use to block that channel. Their US pricing power is the thing at stake.

industries.industry: Canadian pharmacies and wholesale drug distributors
industries.note: The bill creates a certified-seller program that would give licensed Canadian pharmacies and wholesalers a legal export business to US patients and pharmacies, with fees for certification. Their gain runs alongside patients' savings.
Importers registered under the bill could buy qualifying drugs abroad at lower prices and dispense them at home, improving their margins or letting them undercut competitors on price.
The bill permits importation of biosimilars and off-patent products, which could open US market access for foreign-made generics, but also adds new import competition they would have to compete with.
